clinicalPearls: A rare zoonosis caused by the nematode Capillaria hepatica, primarily a parasite of rodents, acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs from soil contaminated with decayed infected animal carcasses
The adult worms and their eggs lodge in the liver parenchyma rather than the gut, so true infection does not produce eggs in the stool
Genuine hepatic capillariasis presents with fever, tender hepatomegaly, abdominal pain and marked eosinophilia, and can progress to hepatic dysfunction
Spurious infection is an important pitfall: eggs pass through the gut and appear in stool after eating infected animal liver, without the person being parasitised
Diagnosis of true disease usually requires liver biopsy demonstrating adult worms and characteristic eggs within the parenchyma
Treatment is with an anthelmintic such as albendazole, often with corticosteroid cover for the inflammatory reaction
Prevention centres on hygiene and avoiding ingestion of soil contaminated by infected rodent carcasses
reference.pathophysiology: Capillaria hepatica is a nematode whose natural cycle involves rodents and other mammals. Adult worms live within the liver parenchyma and deposit eggs directly into the surrounding tissue; these eggs are not released into the intestine and only become infective after the host dies and the carcass decomposes, releasing eggs into the soil where they embryonate. Humans are infected by ingesting these embryonated eggs. Larvae hatch in the intestine, penetrate the wall and travel via the portal circulation to the liver, where they mature and lay eggs. The accumulating worms and egg masses provoke a granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammatory response with focal necrosis and progressive fibrosis of the liver. Because eggs remain trapped in the parenchyma, they are absent from the stool in genuine infection, whereas spurious egg passage occurs harmlessly after eating an infected animal's liver.
additionalDifferentials: Visceral larva migrans (Toxocara) with hepatic involvement
Fascioliasis and other hepatobiliary trematode infection
Other causes of eosinophilic hepatitis or hepatic granulomas
Spurious egg passage after eating infected liver
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count demonstrating marked eosinophilia and leucocytosis
Liver function tests and inflammatory markers
Liver biopsy showing adult worms and characteristic eggs in the parenchyma
Repeat stool examination on a liver-free diet to distinguish true from spurious infection
Abdominal imaging for hepatomegaly and focal hepatic lesions
Serology where available to support the diagnosis
redFlags: Progressive hepatic dysfunction or evolving liver failure
High fever with tender hepatomegaly and marked eosinophilia
Extensive hepatic necrosis or fibrosis on biopsy
Failure to improve, prompting reconsideration of malignancy or other pathology
reference.prognosis: True hepatic capillariasis is a serious infection that can be fatal in heavy or untreated cases, though timely anthelmintic therapy can lead to recovery; spurious infection is entirely benign and requires only recognition.
pitfalls: Diagnosing infection from stool eggs alone, which usually reflects spurious passage rather than true disease
Failing to repeat stool testing on a liver-free diet to exclude spurious eggs
Overlooking liver biopsy as the definitive means of confirming genuine infection
Mistaking the hepatic lesions for abscess or malignancy
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat true infection with an anthelmintic such as albendazole or mebendazole to clear the parasite
Cover the anthelmintic with corticosteroids to dampen the granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammatory reaction as worms die
Provide supportive care for hepatic dysfunction and pain
Confirm genuine parasitism rather than spurious infection before treating, sparing unnecessary therapy where only ingested eggs pass through the gut
Monitor the eosinophil count and liver function to gauge response
Refer to tropical medicine or hepatology and advise hand and food hygiene to avoid ingesting soil-borne embryonated eggs
